definition: Deliberately training a smaller model far past its compute-optimal token count (Llama-style, hundreds of tokens per parameter) because a smaller, better-trained model is cheaper to serve for its quality level.
details: Deliberately training a smaller model far past its compute-optimal token count (Llama-style, hundreds of tokens per parameter) because a smaller, better-trained model is cheaper to serve for its quality level. Training cost is paid once; inference cost is paid forever.

explainer.lead: Overtraining is deliberately training a smaller model far past its compute-optimal token count, in the hundreds of tokens per parameter, because a smaller, better-trained model is cheaper to serve for its quality level. The logic is that training cost is paid once, while inference cost is paid forever.

tiers.eli5: It is like spending extra hours training a smaller, cheaper worker so you never have to hire an expensive one again.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to build small models that match larger ones at inference time, trading up-front compute for long-term serving savings. A pitfall is ignoring the one-time training bill and the diminishing quality returns of extreme token counts.
tiers.paperLevel: Overtraining is training a smaller model well past compute-optimal tokens per parameter (Llama-style, hundreds of tokens per parameter) to lower inference cost for a given quality level; the tradeoff is higher one-time training cost.

explainer.example: A small model trained on hundreds of tokens per parameter serves at a fraction of the cost of a larger model while reaching comparable quality.
